reasoning: Both core defects are real. (1) Design: _find_standalone_libduckdb (utils.py:33) is called as a pure probe by load_duckdb (line 119), before the Darwin check at line 124, but lines 38-40 unconditionally attempt os.remove of a legacy cache file with no caller visibility. The mixing of discovery and mutation in a 'find' function is a genuine design flaw. (2) Unguarded OSError: lines 39-40 are `if os.path.isfile(old_cached): os.remove(old_cached)` with no try/except. A TOCTOU race (concurrent deletion between isfile and remove) raises FileNotFoundError; a permission error on a read-only file raises PermissionError. Either propagates unhandled out of what callers treat as a non-throwing probe and aborts load_duckdb with an error unrelated to the real problem. One sub-claim is overstated: the finding says the destructive cleanup 'runs on Linux/Windows' but os.path.isfile returns False for ~/.numbduck/lib/libduckdb.dylib on Linux in practice (the file is macOS-only), so the actual os.remove does not fire on non-Darwin. The isfile check does run on all platforms, and the absence of a Darwin gate is a real design smell, but the destructive impact on Linux/Windows is theoretical rather than operational. Severity medium is correct: this is a real crash path and a maintainability issue but not a security or data-loss risk (the target file is a cache entry the code itself created).
